title: WhatsApp is a 'lifeline' for refugees. Advocates fear it could be severed in fight over federal bill
summary: Meta said this week that Bill C-22 could force it to "consider" withdrawing encrypted services like WhatsApp from Canada. Rights advocates say that would cut refugees and other newcomers off from a…

image.caption: A Meta representative says the tech giant would 'need to consider' withdrawing services from Canada such as WhatsApp that would be affected by the federal government's lawful access legislation, Bill C-22. (Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters)

blocks.text: When Raymond Gukiina came to Canada in 2022 as a refugee, he used WhatsApp to stay in touch with his family back home in Uganda.
But Gukiina also turned to the popular messaging app to help other refugees and asylum seekers who were struggling to find safe places to live amid a housing crisis in Toronto.

"We opened up a WhatsApp group that had mostly refugees that were sent out of the shelters or living on the streets ... to share information" about shelter beds and other services, the 26-year-old said.

Gukiina, now executive director of the National Network for Immigrants and Refugees-Canada, a non-profit that grew out of the WhatsApp group, said the platform remains key for newcomers to get support in their new communities and maintain ties to loved ones abroad.

But a recent Senate committee hearing has fuelled concerns that a lawful access bill being advanced by the federal government could affect messaging services such as WhatsApp and cut vulnerable people off from the platform they rely on.
Raymond Gukiina says WhatsApp is a key tool for refugees and other newcomers to Canada. (Submitted by Raymond Gukiina)

That's because major tech companies have said they may be forced to suspend services that offer end-to-end encryption if the controversial legislation, known as Bill C-22, which would give law enforcement more access to private communications and data, comes into force.
"Shutting it down [would be] really a tragedy," Gukiina said of WhatsApp.

Alina Murad, director of federal government relations at The Refugee Centre, a non-profit group in Montreal, also described WhatsApp as "a very, very crucial tool" in the refugee resettlement and integration processes.
"It's a lifeline in many ways," she said.
"So if you take away this tool that, for the most part, everyone in the world is familiar with and knows how to use with ease, it leaves people vulnerable — extremely vulnerable."
Meta would consider pulling apps from Canada over 'lawful access' bill
The legislation

Bill C-22, which is being studied in the Senate, would require technology companies to adapt their systems to be able to provide private communications to Canadian law enforcement and the CSIS spy agency during investigations.
Companies would also be forced to retain users' metadata for six months.

The government has said the measures will help create "a modernized legal framework that helps ensure that CSIS can investigate threats to the security of Canada and law enforcement agencies can effectively detect, deter and respond to crime."

But at a Senate committee hearing on Monday, representatives for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, and Signal, another encrypted messaging service, said Bill C-22 would hamper their ability to offer end-to-end encryption in Canada.

items: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is

blocks.text: Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy for Canada, said the company "would need to consider" withdrawing affected services — effectively, WhatsApp — if the legislation passes.

"In a similar situation, when Apple was served with a technical assistance order that it could not comply with without weakening or breaking encryption in the U.K., it chose to withdraw those affected services from the market," she said. "And I think we would need to consider the same option."

Udbhav Tiwari, vice-president of strategy and global affairs at Signal, also told the Senate committee on Monday that the firm would be forced to either "engineer a vulnerability" into its platform or refuse to comply with the law.
"And at that point in time, we will have no choice but not to serve Canadian users."

David Taylor, a spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, told CBC News in an email Friday that the legislation does "not permit or require companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called 'back doors.'"

Amendments adopted in the House of Commons also clarify that "service providers cannot be required to break encryption or introduce systemic vulnerabilities, that ministerial authorities cannot be used in place of judicial warrants and that any data-related requirements are strictly limited to metadata, with reduced retention periods and clear legal thresholds," Taylor said.
"The proposals on encryption in C-22 are similar to those in Australia, where WhatsApp continues to operate. They are stronger than those in the United Kingdom, where WhatsApp is available."
Group chats key
Nevertheless, the legislation has fuelled fears that WhatsApp service could be affected.

WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use its platform. While usage varies by country, a 2023 survey by the U.S.-based Pew Research Center found that it had "broad reach" in middle-income countries in particular.

Ashika Niraula, a senior research associate at Toronto Metropolitan University's Global Migration Institute, studies how highly skilled migrants and international students use digital platforms before and after they get to Canada.
WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use the messaging platform. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)
She said WhatsApp groups — where more than 1,000 people can exchange messages in a single digital space — have emerged as a key place for newcomers to get information about life in Canada.
That ranges from how to rent an apartment, open a bank account or find affordable groceries to navigating the Canadian immigration process.

The group chats help newcomers feel less isolated while creating a place to speak openly with people who share their cultural backgrounds or languages and have gone through similar experiences, Niraula said.
"It can help [make] settling into a new country feel less overwhelming."
Encryption offers 'level of safety'

At the same time, WhatsApp remains an easy and cost-effective way for newcomers to stay in touch with relatives in their home countries, said Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees.
"Not being able to get back in touch with your family members who you've been separated from" can have very real effects, including on peoples' mental health, she said.

blocks.text: "If it's no longer possible to use WhatsApp in Canada but it continues to be available across most other countries ... there's a sense of people in Canada being left behind."
Lallemand also said the fact that WhatsApp is encrypted "provides some level of safety" for people who fled persecution in their home countries — and losing that encryption could put them at risk.

"People who are journalists, human rights defenders, refugees in Canada — they often already face repression transnationally, like surveillance threats and intimidation by foreign governments," she said.
"So it is doubly dangerous to be introducing laws that could further target communities that are already very vulnerable."
